roles.title: Backend engineer
roles.blurb: You own logic other services call and then trust. Nobody reads your code — they read a number on a screen and decide whether to believe the company. Your failures are quiet, which is what makes them expensive.
roles.you_tend_to_own: validation, business rules, and the figures other teams report off

roles.title: Frontend engineer
roles.blurb: You own the two edges of the system a human actually touches: what they hand you, and what you show them afterwards. Everything you display is a claim, and you are usually not the one who computed it.
roles.you_tend_to_own: input contracts, and the surfaces that render somebody else's output

roles.title: Computer-vision engineer
roles.blurb: You own a decision made from pixels. The model is rarely the hard part — the hard part is deciding what counts as a detection, and what you do when you are not sure.
roles.you_tend_to_own: detection, the confidence threshold, and when to escalate to a human

roles.title: Platform engineer
roles.blurb: You own the parts nobody thanks you for until they are missing: where the data comes in, where it is kept, and whether anyone can reconstruct afterwards what actually happened.
roles.you_tend_to_own: capture, durable storage, and the audit trail

roles.title: Data engineer
roles.blurb: You move data and reshape it, and you have to be able to prove later what it looked like on the way through. Ordering and idempotency are not features of the job — they are the job.
roles.you_tend_to_own: ingest, deduplication, normalisation, and the write path

domains.title: Web service / API
domains.blurb: Something other teams call over HTTP and then depend on. The work is mostly correctness under inputs you did not choose, and the failures are quiet — a wrong number ships and nobody notices for a week.

domains.title: Vision system
domains.blurb: A camera, a model, and a decision. The hard part is almost never the model: it is deciding what counts as a detection, and what you do when you are not sure.

domains.title: Data pipeline
domains.blurb: Move data, reshape it, and be able to prove afterwards what it looked like on the way through. Ordering and idempotency are the entire job.

projects.title: Checkout pricing service
projects.why_exemplary: Every commerce company has this exact function, and it is the one place where an off-by-a-little bug turns into refunds and a finance escalation rather than a stack trace. It is also small enough to hold in your head, which is what makes the ordering mistake inside it so instructive.

roles.title: Backend engineer — pricing
roles.one_liner: You own the four steps between a cart and a number finance reports off.

roles.title: Frontend engineer — checkout
roles.one_liner: You own the cart the pricing service is called with, and the receipt the customer reads.

projects.title: Site safety-gear check
projects.why_exemplary: A real deployment shape: a camera on a site entrance, a decision per person, and a consequence for being wrong in either direction. False negatives are a safety incident and false positives get the system switched off by the people it is meant to protect — so the interesting engineering is entirely in the ordering of the checks.

roles.title: CV engineer — detection and decision
roles.one_liner: You own who is in frame, whether they are wearing a helmet, and when to raise an alert.

roles.title: Platform engineer — capture and audit
roles.one_liner: You own the camera feed the detector reads, the incident log it writes to, and the screen an auditor opens.

projects.title: Idempotent event ingest
projects.why_exemplary: The canonical distributed-systems lesson in a form small enough to finish: the same event arrives twice and your job is for that to be boring. Almost every candidate can describe idempotency and almost none have implemented it.

roles.title: Data engineer — ingest
roles.one_liner: You own everything between the webhook handing you an event and the row that lands in the table.
